bib.title: Incentivizing Agentic Reasoning in LLM Judges via Tool-Integrated Reinforcement Learning

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 24 pages read (80,181 chars extracted), including appendices A-F and tables. References skimmed. Figures 3-6 are plots only; their values are not in the extraction. No embedded instructions found.

SOURCE: "Incentivizing Agentic Reasoning in LLM Judges via Tool-Integrated Reinforcement Learning" (TIR-Judge). First author Ran Xu (Emory University and Google; work done during a Google internship). Co-authors: Jingjing Chen, Jiayu Ye, Yu Wu (Google), Jun Yan (Google Cloud AI Research), Carl Yang (Emory), Hongkun Yu (Google). arXiv:2510.23038v2 [cs.CL], 21 Feb 2026. The page header is dated 2026-02-24. No venue is stated, so treat it as a preprint.

CORE CLAIM: A judge model that writes and runs Python while judging, and is trained end-to-end with RL, beats text-only reasoning judges. Counting words or letters, checking constraints, arithmetic and running tests are done exactly by code. The model is also trained to skip the tool where it does not help, such as safety and general helpfulness prompts. Variants:
- TIR-Judge-Zero: no distillation. Loop of RL, then rejection sampling, then SFT, then RL.
- TIR-Judge-Distill: SFT on about 10k Gemini-2.5-Flash tool trajectories, then RL.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Abstract: "surpasses strong reasoning-based judges by up to 6.4% (pointwise) and 7.7% (pairwise)". The paper does not say whether these are absolute points or relative. Setup: seven benchmarks, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbones, about 26k training pairs (26,361), single run, no variance reported.
2. PPE Correctness (Table 1): TIR-Judge beats similar-size baselines by 4.8%-9.9% pointwise and 4.5%-8.8% pairwise. It matches RRM-32B on PPE and RewardBench with 1/4 to 1/8 of the parameters.
3. Listwise on RewardBench2, best-of-4, 5 subsets (Table 2): TIR-Judge-Zero 8B averages 73.4 and Claude-Opus-4 76.5, which the paper calls "96%" (73.4/76.5 is about 96%). For comparison: Gemini-2.5-flash-Preview 75.9, TIR-Judge-Distill 8B 71.6, GPT-4.1 69.7, Claude-Sonnet-4 69.5, GPT-4o 64.9. On the IF subset TIR-Judge-Distill 8B scores 58.1 against 41.9 for Opus-4. Opus-4 is far better on Fact (82.7 against 64.8 for Zero 8B).
4. Tools alone do not help. Prompting Qwen-3 with the same code tool gives "negligible (<1%) or even negative gains"; RL is what unlocks tool use. Per Table 1, Qwen3-8B-Tool pointwise averages 59.4 against 64.9 for plain Qwen3-8B pointwise. Pairwise averages: TIR-Judge-Zero 8B 72.0, Zero 4B 73.7, Distill 8B 72.6, Distill 4B 70.5. Pointwise: Zero 4B 70.4, Distill 4B 66.7, Distill 8B 68.2, Zero 8B 67.5.
5. Zero versus Distill: Zero is better on 4/6 benchmarks (pointwise) and 3/6 (pairwise). The intro says Zero gains 1.2% over Distill at 4B. Table 1 does not agree: the 4B pairwise average is 73.7 against 70.5 (Distill), and at 8B pairwise Distill leads, 72.6 against 72.0. Check the 1.2% before citing it.
6. Best-of-N (Fig 4b, Table 7): on AIME and BigCodeBench, TIR-Judge-Zero gains 3.9-6.7% absolute over RRM-7B. For example, BigCodeBench Deepseek-Coder (1139 problems) passes 285 at Pass@1, 328 with MV@16, and 435 with 4B pointwise Zero. 16 samples per problem, 16k token limit.
7. Cost (Table 8, 8×H100): Zero takes 29.0h and about $690. Distill takes 11.0h and about $340 ($210 compute plus $130 teacher API). Zero is about 2× the cost.

VERBATIM QUOTES
- p.1 (abstract): "most LLM judges operate solely on intrinsic text-based reasoning, limiting their ability to verify complex constraints or perform accurate computation."
- p.8: "Simply augmenting Qwen-3 models with code execution yields negligible (<1%) or even negative gains. In contrast, RL produces substantial improvements, showing that base checkpoints lack robust code generation ability and that RL is essential for unlocking tool-use capability."
- p.4: the reference answer is unseen at evaluation time (footnote 1).

LIMITS
- Tools are code execution only. Gains are concentrated in verifiable tasks: instruction following, math and code.
- Text-only judges did slightly better on Chat and Safety in RM-Bench (Fig 4a).
- Gemini-2.5-Flash sometimes got worse with tools because of the max-turn limit and runaway tool calls (App. B).
- Accuracy only. There is no evaluation of bias, position bias or calibration. Pairwise uses a single random ordering.
- Training data includes synthetic pairs from Qwen3 and Gemma models, and the reward model for preference labels is the benchmark's ground truth. Eight-gram decontamination was applied.
- Only Qwen3 4B/8B backbones. Baseline numbers are partly copied from other papers (marked †).
- Several baselines >10B (RRM-32B, RM-R1-32B) still score higher on many benchmarks.
- The authors do not claim to have found a way to detect when a tool is needed beyond a no-tool format heuristic for safety and helpfulness.
- The authors name future work: more tools and tasks, and using the judge to train policy models.

BUILDS ON
- Tool-integrated reasoning RL: Li et al. 2025b, Feng et al. 2025, Xue et al. 2025 (SimpleTIR), Jin et al. 2025, Bai et al. 2025.
- RL algorithm: DAPO (Yu et al. 2025a), a GRPO variant (Shao et al. 2024).
- RL-trained text judges: J1 (Whitehouse et al. 2025), RM-R1 (Chen et al. 2025b), RRM (Guo et al. 2025b), Think-RM (Hong et al. 2025).
- Tool-assisted judging: Findeis et al. 2025, AgentRM (Peng et al. 2025), Li et al. 2024b.
- Self-bootstrapping: STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022), Singh et al. 2024.
- Verl-Tool (Jiang et al. 2025a) for implementation.
- Benchmarks: PPE, RewardBench, RewardBench 2, RM-Bench, JudgeBench, IFBench, CodeJudgeBench.

BEST-FIT SECTION in 05-llm-as-judge.md: "Known biases", as a counterpoint on judge accuracy (text-only judges hallucinate counts), or a new short subsection after it on "Judges with tools / verifiable checks". "When a judge is the right tool" is the second choice. The prompt-writing sections are not a fit.

FIGURE: Figure 1 (p.1) shows a text-only judge claiming a poem has 392 words, while the code-executing judge counts 321 and fails it. Figure 2 (p.4) shows the training framework. Table 4 (p.11) is a worked IFEval example (counting the letter "O") that makes the same point.
